paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Built to be graceful, modern, and powerful, the American public enthusiastically embraced the SS United States, which became known as 'America's Flagship.' Once upon a time, it carried princes and other powerful men across the Atlantic Ocean in high style and at great speed. The ship's withdrawal from service in 1969 stunned her officers and crew: some left their equipment and personal items on board in anticipation of returning to work the next day, only to find the doors sealed shut. Then it was towed to Ukraine where the interior that once included luxurious cabins and ballrooms was torn out to remove dangerous materials. And since 1996, the steamship SS United States has been tied to a Delaware River pier, in a busy port near a Philadelphia shopping area, while chunks of paint peel off its black hull.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Turning the SS United States into scrap metal would destroy a piece of American social history. It still holds the record for the fastest trans-Atlantic crossing by an ocean liner. The ship, which made its first voyage in July 1952, set the record of 3 days, 10 hours and 40 minutes for an eastbound crossing of the Atlantic at an average of 44 miles per hour. Henry Goldsmith, who sailed on the ship in 1952 when he was 11 years old, recalled the high standard of service, food and entertainment for first-class passengers, who saw first-run movies and could listen to several orchestras. He said that he and his brother were required to wear suits and ties at dinner, and passengers were well-dressed even when strolling the decks. Inside the ship, cabins were once occupied by British royals, American presidents and Hollywood actors. In the ballroom, famous jazz musicians played for first-class passengers, including some of the wealthiest businessmen and their wives, dressed in formal suits and ball gowns.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The high standards of the ship's construction have ensured its structural viability. Tests indicated that its steel retained 92 percent of its integrity. The construction of the ship's superstructure involved the greatest use of aluminum in any construction project to that time, a key point resulting in a significantly lighter vessel. To minimize the risk of fire, the designers of the SS United States used no wood in the ship's framing, accessories, decorations, or interior surfaces. Fittings, including all furniture and fabrics, were custom made in glass and metal to ensure compliance with fireproofing guidelines. The clothes hangers in the luxury cabins were aluminum. Even the ballroom's grand piano was of a rare, fire-resistant wood species – although originally specified in aluminum – and accepted only after a demonstration in which gasoline was poured upon the wood and ignited, without the wood itself igniting.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Now, the 990-foot-long (300-meter) ocean liner that crossed the Atlantic from 1952 until 1969 is the focus of what its owner, the SS United States Conservancy, says is a final effort to save it from demolition. Eighty-two percent of the Conservancy's budget goes to costs that include pier rental, maintenance and insurance. The group had generated income by putting up for sale metal from some areas of the ship that were not historically significant. Simply keeping the ship tied up in Philadelphia is expensive, and that has drained the Conservancy's resources to the point where redevelopment is the only option. Despite the ship's historic listing, the Conservancy receives no government funding.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: If the SS United States is to survive, the Conservancy will need to attract the attention of long-term investors. Without the original walls and partitions that created the environment for passengers to sail between America and Europe in style, the SS United States offers many possibilities for developers to create businesses that will allow the ship to survive. Saying the ship could be only months away from being broken up, the Conservancy is in talks with three developers about its potential to become a complex of hotels, museums, shopping malls and restaurants, or some combination of all options for reuse.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: All potential developers would move the ship to New York where it would likely generate the most income. The group which bought the ship from Norwegian Cruise Line in 2011 also considered docking it in Miami, Baltimore, and Boston, but no other port can match the economic potential that New York offers. New York is also a fitting home for the SS United States as it served as the ship's home port historically.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The ship's future may have parallels with the Rotterdam, another liner that sailed the Atlantic for the Holland America Line from 1959 until 1997, and is now used for mixed purposes in its home port. After leaving service as a liner, the Rotterdam was bought by a Dutch government-backed company and converted into spaces for businesses. Since 2010, it has been occupied by shops and restaurants, a theater, conference facilities and a hotel, which together attract about 500,000 visitors a year. The Rotterdam's businesses overall are profitable, and the SS United States may have the same results due to New York's many tourists.

groups.title: SS United States: 'America's Flagship'
content: The SS United States, also known as 'America's Flagship', was at one time the pride of American commercial shipping. It was famous for crossing the Atlantic Ocean with great elegance as well as {{23}} . It is a piece of American history; however, it is now kept in a {{24}} with no certain future. Due to limited resources of the SS United States Conservancy that is in charge of preserving it, the ship faces possible {{25}} if no alternative use can be found. One possibility for the ship is to allow developers to buy it and change its use entirely, converting it to a dining and tourism complex. Moving it to New York with the city's many tourists would give it the greatest possibility to become {{26}} like the Rotterdam, thereby saving the ship.
